A 4–6 MONTH RESEARCH PROGRAM Joint Standoﬀ Estimation and Magnetic Reconstruction A practical research playbook for quantum diamond microscopy Research question Can a physics-based learned inverse jointly estimate eﬀective standoﬀ and reconstruct a mag- netic image at a speciﬁed reference plane, while generalizing across unseen source geometries, ﬁelds of view, pixel spacings, and noise conditions? Prepared for: Abhay’s micro-coil reconstruction project, with access to COMSOL, GPUs, real QDM measurements, and Anuj Bathla’s experimental dataset. Level: advanced theory and implementation; prerequisites are refreshed where they aﬀect scientiﬁc validity. Primary target: near-plane magnetic ﬁelds. Current density is developed as an optional latent physical representation; this choice can be revised after the dataset audit. Version: 8 October 2026. How to use this document Follow the numbered experiments and decision gates. Build a simple baseline, diagnose its fail- ure, and then introduce one architectural change that addresses that failure. Proposed methods are hypotheses to test, not established novel contributions. No research outcome or conference acceptance is promised. Joint calibration and reconstruction 1 Start with a tractable research claim 1.1 The project you are actually building Your long-term objective is reliable reconstruction of sharp QDM magnetic images under uncertain measurement geometry. The ﬁrst paper should answer a bounded version: for a single planar source layer, can joint standoﬀ inference improve reconstruction of the magnetic ﬁeld at a ﬁxed reference plane, including on source geometries excluded from training? FOV, sampling, and noise robustness become explicit challenge sets. Multilayer separation and optical inversion are later extensions with diﬀerent identiﬁability assumptions. You have access to an extensive existing COMSOL database, GPUs, real QDM measurements, and the experimental dataset underlying Bathla et al. [17]. Use these resources as the core of the study. The few geometries visible in the current repository do not describe the full database available to your group. This guide has not inspected that external database: counts, units, available components, calibrated heights, and acquisition labels must be established by the audit in Section 3. A one-sentence working claim We investigate a joint calibration-and-reconstruction method that uses analytical propagation and a learned source prior to estimate eﬀective standoﬀ and reconstruct a near-plane magnetic ﬁeld, with source-level holdouts and calibrated treatment of ambiguous observations. 1.2 Four hypotheses to investigate separately 1. H1: calibration matters. Height errors explain a measurable part of reconstruction error after boundary and sampling eﬀects are controlled. 2. H2: joint inference helps. Reﬁning image and distance together improves over a height predictor followed by a ﬁxed reconstruction network under matched training data and compute. 3. H3: ambiguity should be represented. A distribution or set of height–image hypotheses yields fewer conﬁdently incorrect decisions than a single estimate. 4. H4: physical metadata helps transfer. Explicit observation operators and physical pixel spacing improve transfer across FOV and sampling changes. H1 can be rejected. H2 can be rejected. A simple baseline winning is useful information. Choose one central methodological claim for the paper; treat the other hypotheses as controls or supporting studies. 1 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction 1.3 Use the guide in passes Pass Read and execute Required output before expanding scope First 10 days Scope, dataset audit, E00–E03 Weeks 3–6 Baselines and architecture A0–A3 Weeks 7–12 One proposed mechanism; challenge sets Real-data validation and paper evidence Trusted operator; wrong-height curve; source split A clear baseline failure and an interpretable prototype Matched ablation with repeatable beneﬁt Defensible physical claim, limitations, reproducible release Months 4–6 Deliverable Your immediate milestone is one ﬁgure showing reconstruction error and observation mismatch versus assumed height, evaluated on several independent COMSOL source layouts. 2 Physics, observations, and identiﬁability 2.1 Deﬁne the output before deﬁning the network Let h be the sensor height relative to a declared source plane, and let z ref be the ﬁxed target-plane height. Initially use z ref = 0.5 µm to match the repository. The propagation gap is δ = h − z ref > 0. Let x denote the vector ﬁeld at that plane on a larger physical domain, before restricting it to the requested output ROI. The observation is y = CSQA δ x + η = M h x + η. (1) Here Q projects onto measured NV axes or selects vector components; S integrates/resamples to detector pixels; C restricts the observation window; and η denotes noise. Known optical and NV-depth averaging can eventually enter M h . They should be accounted for as nuisance eﬀects when material, even while optical deconvolution remains outside the ﬁrst paper. For simulation inputs, y can contain all three signed components. The published Bathla acquisition uses a single NV-axis projection. A model must support the actual available channels; a single-axis image cannot be relabelled as three independently measured components. The primary target is a magnetic ﬁeld, not an optical photograph or binary wire segmentation. Generate the physical ﬁeld on a larger domain before sensing and cropping. The learned inverse estimates the target ﬁeld and calibration parameters from the observed map. 2 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction 2.2 Analytical propagation and sensitivity to distance In a homogeneous source-free region, ∇ × H = 0 and ∇ · H = 0. The scalar potential is harmonic. For spatial frequency f = (f x , f y ) in cycles per micrometre, b (f , z 2 ) = e −2π∥f ∥(z 2 −z 1 ) x b (f , z 1 ). x (2) The three signed components share this decay. In vacuum, B = µ 0 H; store which quantity and units are supplied. In this project the cache is in tesla and loading typically converts to microtesla. B norm is nonlinear and should not be treated as another independent linear measurement channel. H δ (f ) = e −2π∥f ∥δ , ∂ h H δ = −2π ∥f ∥ H δ . A common symmetric-log colour scale exposes both attenuation and broadening; peak values are stated explicitly. This example teaches observation physics, not the proposed coil benchmark. 2.3 An exact reason that residual-only height estimation fails In an ideal inﬁnite-plane, noiseless model, suppose y = A δ x. For any 0 ≤ δ ′ ≤ δ, deﬁne x ′ = A δ−δ ′ x. The semigroup property gives A δ ′ x ′ = A δ ′ A δ−δ ′ x = A δ x = y. (4) Thus a smoother reference ﬁeld at a smaller gap explains the same observation exactly. A ﬂexible unconstrained ﬁeld can trade source structure against distance. A network trained on one coil size may learn that size as a shortcut and call larger coils “farther away.” Restrictions to real source families, geometric knowledge, controlled drive currents, and indepen- dent calibration can make height inference informative. A learned estimate is conditional on those assumptions. Physical consistency and extra vector channels improve practical constraints but do not guarantee unique absolute depth for unrestricted planar sources. 2.4 Proﬁle objectives and nuisance parameters A useful diagnostic is n Φ(h) = min x 2 1 2 ∥W (M h x − y)∥ + λR(x) o , (5) where W whitens the assumed noise. Plot Φ(h), its data term, and ground-truth reconstruction error separately. Proﬁle minima depend on the prior, noise model, support, and solver accuracy; a proﬁle is not automatically a calibrated posterior. For local source parameters ϑ, deﬁne the whitened sensitivities J h = ∂ h (W M h x ϑ ) and J ϑ = ∂ ϑ (W M h x ϑ ). A local nuisance-adjusted information diagnostic is I h|ϑ = J h T (I − P J ϑ )J h , (6) with P the projection onto the nuisance sensitivity span. If distance changes can be reproduced by changing geometry or current, little information remains. This is a local idealized diagnostic; nonlinear multimodality and model error require explicit tests. 2.5 What additional heights actually provide Measurements at several heights above all sources are related by upward continuation in the ideal complete-plane source-free model. They do not independently determine an arbitrary multilayer decomposition. In practice they can improve SNR, registration checks, noise characterization, and ﬁnite-window constraints. Known stage increments give relative distances; absolute standoﬀ remains a separate calibration question. 4 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction 2.6 A minimal physically constrained source representation For planar currents, a stream function g can deﬁne J x = ∂ y g and J y = −∂ x g, enforcing ∇ · J = 0 away from contacts. Predicting g and using Biot–Savart provides a source-aware prior, then the ﬁeld at z ref becomes the main output. Contacts and currents crossing the FOV require appropri- ate source-domain extensions and boundary treatment. Field-ﬁrst and source-latent formulations should be compared, not silently conﬂated. Scientiﬁc interpretation Standoﬀ deblurring restores detail conditional on a prior and measurement model. A ﬁner output grid is not evidence of ﬁner physical resolution. Deﬁne success through recoverable features, ﬁeld accuracy, calibration accuracy, and reliability on held-out sources. 3 Audit and organize the existing databases 3.1 Your resources and the ﬁrst decisions The user conﬁrmed an existing detailed COMSOL database and access to the real measurements from Bathla et al. [17]. The experimental ﬁles are on external storage and will be obtained later; their contents have not yet been inspected. The ﬁrst-paper output is conﬁrmed as near-plane magnetic ﬁelds, with currents used as an auxiliary model. Begin the simulation study immediately; make the real-data protocols conditional on the audit rather than postponing the entire project. 3.2 COMSOL inventory: the ﬁrst two working days Make a read-only manifest before conversion. Give each source layout a stable geometry_id, and each simulation conﬁguration a scene_id. Distinguish a genuinely new conductor layout from a diﬀerent height, current, mesh, or crop of the same layout. Count unique geometries, not exported images. Required ﬁeld Purpose and veriﬁcation Geometry/source identity Coordinates and pitch Height convention CAD/model hash; topology; turns; width; spacing; source layer; contacts. Identify duplicates and translated copies. Physical x, y, z coordinates; ascending order; exact ∆x, ∆y; FOV extent. Verify orientation and registration. Origin of z; conductor top, centre, or substrate reference; known source thickness; absolute height versus gap. Applied current/voltage; measured or prescribed value; sign; contact boundary conditions. B versus H; units; material permeability; current density availability; source-free region validity. COMSOL version, mesh size, solver tolerance, interpolation/export procedure, simulation boundaries. Paths, SHA-256, grid shape, data type, component labels, missing values, source-generation seed. Field at z ref ; existence of complete same-geometry height sweeps; whether a trusted target needs new simulation. Drive Physics and quantity Numerics Files and provenance Target availability 5 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction Create a report showing height counts per geometry, pitch/FOV distributions, missing compo- nents, ﬁeld ranges, and coordinate agreement. Plot a few proﬁles at every height. Repeated ﬁeld interpolation artifacts are model discrepancy, not automatically independent measurement noise. 3.3 Reuse complete height sweeps without learning test-pair kernels Where a geometry has ﬁelds at z ref and several higher planes, use the lower ﬁeld as target and each higher plane as an observation. The analytical operator is evaluated from physical spacing and height. A held-out sharp ﬁeld must not be used to ﬁt that observation’s empirical kernel. Compare direct COMSOL high-plane ﬁelds with analytical propagation of the low-plane ﬁeld. This residual includes export interpolation, discretization, ﬁnite-window error, registration, and any modelling mismatch. Investigate its structure before ascribing it to mesh noise. A bounded empirical correction may be a later experiment, but its parameters must be ﬁtted on training/cal- ibration data only, and tested on unused geometries or acquisition sessions. 3.4 Dataset tiers Tier Data Scientiﬁc role T0: mechanics Small analytical cases, Fourier Operator, adjoint, gradients, and modes, closed loops ambiguity checks T1: pilot Stratiﬁed subset of the existing Baseline comparison and failure COMSOL database discovery T2: challenge Disjoint COMSOL layouts/families Generalization; simulator/model and selected numerical settings mismatch T3: real archive Audited Bathla maps, labels, and Real noise, dictionary comparison, repetitions source activations T4: new Calibrated height sweeps and Direct validation of target-plane acquisition independent layouts reconstruction and distance Use new analytical scenes to answer controlled questions, not as a replacement for the existing database. Add new COMSOL simulations only to ﬁll an identiﬁed gap: geometry families, near- plane references, mesh-convergence checks, or height ranges. 3.5 Splitting protocol and leakage controls First assign source identities to train, validation, calibration, and test groups; only then derive heights, current rescalings, crops, and noise variants. The calibration group is needed only if uncertainty calibration is included and must be distinct from the model-selection validation set. All descendants of a geometry remain in the same group. Near-duplicates and variants from the same template generator may require a higher-level family grouping. Maintain two diﬀerent evaluations: new-instance interpolation within a geometry family, and unseen-family transfer. A random split of conﬁgurations is not evidence of unseen geometry. Separate height interpolation from extrapolation. Record exact withheld ranges and test them once after selecting the model. For a pilot, choose approximately 100 independent layouts if available, with a 60/20/20 source-level train/validation/test split. This is a starting engineering conﬁguration, not a sample-size justiﬁ- cation. If calibration is needed, reserve additional sources or repartition without examining the locked test outcomes. Expand according to learning curves and precision of source-level conﬁdence intervals. 6 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction Independent source/- CAD identities and acquisition sessions Training sources Validation and calibration sources Locked test sources All heights, crops, noise descendants All heights, crops, noise descendants All heights, crops, noise descendants Figure 5: Split physical identities before creating training examples. Correlated crops and height variants cannot be moved across source-level partitions. 3.6 Sampling, cropping, and normalization Propagate on a larger domain and then apply pixel integration and FOV restriction. For coarser pitch, antialias and integrate the ﬁeld; do not simply resize an image and declare a new physical spacing. Upsampling labels does not create new measured information. If the target uses a diﬀerent grid, make that output grid explicit and interpolate only through a documented observation model. Use a ﬁxed scale estimated from training data or an observation-only scale q(y), and retain q as physical metadata when amplitude carries information. Reconstruct in physical units for metrics. If minimizing the existing half-squared loss plus an L1 penalty under x = qu, the normalized coeﬃcient is λ/q. Do not normalize using held-out sharp targets. At zero or near-zero signal, use a predetermined scale ﬂoor and ﬂag height as uninformative. Rotating a ﬁeld image requires rotating its vector components as well as its spatial coordinates. Under a planar rotation R, rotate (B x , B y ) consistently and transform the NV projection direction for scalar observations. Scaling geometry changes physics and cannot be implemented by spatial resizing alone. Reverse all signed components for current reversal under the linear magnetostatic model. 4 How to use Anuj Bathla’s experimental dataset 4.1 What is established and what is still unknown The published study describes measured individual-coil basis ﬁelds and mixed activations on a multilayer micro-coil platform, plus time-dependent measurements. Its reconstruction uses sparse coeﬃcients in a measured dictionary. Your group’s original ﬁles may contain more information than the paper, but this guide cannot assume that ﬁxed-reference sharp ﬁelds, absolute calibrated standoﬀs, or all vector components are already present. Obtain those facts from acquisition logs. 4.2 Data-receipt checklist 1. Copy data into a read-only archive; retain original folder structure, checksums, and the acqui- sition notebook. Work from versioned derived copies. 2. Identify ﬁeld maps, raw ODMR/lock-in sequences, current-on/oﬀ references, individual-coil maps, mixed activations, timestamps, and event waveforms. 7 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction 3. Obtain the coil-to-layer lookup, microscope magniﬁcation, pixel pitch, NV axis, coordinate conventions, drive values, and registration transforms. 4. Label every distance as independently measured, nominal, model-ﬁtted, relative stage displace- ment, or unknown. Store uncertainty and calibration method. 5. Ask whether basis maps and mixtures were measured in the same session and at the same drive. Check drift, gain, and background diﬀerences. 6. Verify data-release permission and what can be made public. This aﬀects the reproducibility package; it does not alter the scientiﬁc split. 4.3 Six concrete uses, in increasing order of diﬃculty U1: benchmark the published task. Reproduce ﬁeld ﬁtting and activation recovery with the measured dictionary before adding a neural network. The unknown is a coeﬃcient vector, not ﬁeld pixels. For dictionary D = [d 1 , . . . , d K ] and observation y, solve ĉ = arg min 12 ∥W (Dc − y)∥ 2 + λ ∥c∥ 1 . c (7) Use NNLS only if nonnegative currents are physically justiﬁed. Compare coeﬃcient error, activa- tion precision/recall, and ﬁeld residuals. This is a calibration and reproducibility exercise, not a new research claim. U2: learn experimental noise. Repetitions and current-oﬀ acquisitions can estimate spatial variance, correlations, drift, and ﬁtting uncertainty. Subtracting a spatially varying physical ﬁeld is not equivalent to measuring noise. Split sessions so repeated backgrounds do not leak. Where raw ODMR ﬁts provide covariance, propagate it or use it to weight the observation loss. U3: calibrate simulator-to-measurement discrepancy. Match known CAD and drive set- tings to measured individual-coil ﬁelds. Fit limited nuisance parameters such as global registration, axis angle, gain, and eﬀective distance on a calibration subset. Do not allow a free learned kernel to absorb every error. Test ﬁtted corrections on unused coils or sessions. U4: experimentally adapt a pretrained ﬁeld prior. Start from COMSOL supervision. Use repeated real observations, known source activations, and correctly modelled measurement consistency to adapt on an explicit adaptation set. Validate on separate acquisitions. A dictionary- generated Dc is a model-based surrogate at the sensor plane, not an independent near-plane truth. Shared noisy basis maps can correlate surrogate target and input noise. U5: construct a real dictionary LISTA baseline. Train an unrolled sparse-code network for c on activation labels and compare with LASSO at matched inference latency. This tests learned acceleration and provides a source-aware auxiliary branch. It does not directly establish standoﬀ super-resolution. Hold out activation patterns for known-dictionary performance; hold out source identities or a new array for geometry transfer. U6: validate near-plane reconstruction. If the archive contains registered measurements at several calibrated positions, form higher-to-lower-plane test pairs with the same optics. Otherwise acquire new height sweeps. Do not invent sharp references by applying your own inverse to the archive and then evaluate against them. 4.4 Splits that are honest for a single fabricated array Holding out activation combinations tests combinatorial generalization for known source templates. All combinations on one array are not independent new geometries. A shared dictionary may be legitimate calibration information in that task, but it must be declared and kept separate 8 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction Bathla experimental archive audit labels and calibration Basis maps + mixtures dictionary/activation benchmark Raw/repeated acquisitions noise and do- main adaptation Coeﬃcients and sensor-plane ﬁelds are useful supervision Calibrated height pairs validate near- plane prediction Figure 6: Diﬀerent experimental data support diﬀerent claims. Activate a branch only after the necessary metadata and measurements are veriﬁed. from unseen-geometry claims. Use held-out acquisition sessions to test drift. For dynamics, split contiguous events/runs and leave guard intervals; neighbouring frames are strongly correlated. If a known-coil dictionary is available at test time, report that regime separately from “no per-coil calibration.” Holding out a coil while secretly supplying its measured basis is not unknown-source generalization. For unseen coils, use CAD-based physical templates or new independent arrays and disclose the information provided. Scientiﬁc interpretation A known activation vector can label which source was driven; it does not necessarily give an exact current amplitude or a unique multilayer current map. Model-assisted labels, nominal heights, and independently measured targets should appear as separate evidence tiers. Deliverable Produce two manifests, a source/session split ﬁle, a dictionary reproduction report, and a list of missing metadata or acquisitions needed for the primary near-plane claim. 5 The experiment ladder: investigate before inventing Each experiment should have a short conﬁguration ﬁle, immutable split identiﬁer, source revision, arrays, metrics, and a visual report. Work through E00–E05 ﬁrst. The remaining experiments are selected by the observed failure, rather than executed as an indiscriminate architecture sweep. 5.1 E00: operator correctness and model discrepancy Question. Does the observation operator represent the data well enough that a new network is scientiﬁcally interpretable? Procedure. Check Fourier-mode attenuation, identity at zero gap, nonnegative upward gaps, padding/cropping, pixel integration, component projection, and transpose ordering. Verify ⟨M h x, r⟩ = ⟨x, M ∗ h r⟩ on asymmetric grids and masks. Compare the autograd derivative in h with centred ﬁnite diﬀerences on a small problem. Compare independent COMSOL high-plane ﬁelds with propagated reference ﬁelds, using interior and full-FOV metrics. Controls. Increase physical-domain size/padding; reﬁne one representative COMSOL mesh; com- 9 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction pare registered coordinates. Test double precision on a small case before using GPU ﬂoat32. If error changes with window size, do not call it solely simulation noise. Output. Adjoint/gradient errors, component residual maps, residual spectra, interior-versus- boundary error, and a model-discrepancy summary. This step is a necessary numerical veriﬁcation, not a novel result by itself. 5.2 E01: known-height reconstruction Question. What detail is recoverable when calibration is available? Run analytic ﬁltered inversion, classical regularized reconstruction, the repository’s LISTA with physics corrections, and a small supervised residual CNN or U-Net on the same source split. Use the true height only in the explicitly labelled known-height controls. Tune cutoﬀs and penalties on validation sources. Evaluate every component, a predeﬁned source ROI, proﬁles, and latency. Compare ﬁeld-pixel L1, quadratic smoothness, wavelet sparsity, and vector TV as distinct priors. For vector TV one possible deﬁnition is R VTV (x) = X p s X [(D x x c ) 2 p + (D y x c ) 2 p ] + ε 2TV . (8) c Choose ﬁnite-diﬀerence spacing in physical units. An arbitrary CNN denoiser is not automatically a proximal operator, and its iterations do not inherit FISTA’s convex convergence guarantee. Decision gate If known-height methods cannot recover the target on the pilot, investigate noise, sampling, source prior, or model mismatch before introducing height estimation. A known-height control is an information reference, not a universal accuracy upper bound. 5.3 E02: intentionally wrong height Question. How much does calibration error aﬀect reconstruction, and can residuals diagnose it? Select low, medium, and high heights from the actual database and multiple independent layouts. Sweep assumed height around each true value, subject to h > z ref . For an observation at 3 µm, an illustrative sweep is 2 to 4 µm with ﬁner samples near 3 µm. Reconstruct to the same declared solver tolerance at each candidate. Reuse warm starts only if their eﬀect and timing are recorded. Plot reconstruction error, whitened observation mismatch, regularization cost, and feature/proﬁle error against assumed height. Repeat at zero noise and two speciﬁed physical noise levels. Show cases where a good residual accompanies a poor reconstruction. Interpretation. A broad residual valley is consistent with ambiguity; a narrow prior-dependent objective minimum does not establish true height. A monotone preference for the lowest permitted height may reﬂect the semigroup degeneracy. Use this experiment to set application-relevant error tolerances rather than inventing a success threshold after seeing test data. 5.4 E03: source–height ambiguity and shortcut detection Question. Which changes in source parameters can imitate a height change? Vary source size, track width, turns, spacing, location, and current independently of height. Find nearest observation pairs from diﬀerent layouts/heights using a noise-weighted distance. For Gaus- sian noise a likelihood comparison uses the whitened separation Σ −1/2 (y 1 − y 2 ) ; interpret it 10 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction under the actual covariance and sampling, not raw pixel count. Verify lookalike cases visually and using proﬁles. Train a minimal height predictor. Evaluate it on held-out size ranges, current amplitudes, and shape families. Compare physical units, observation-only normalization with retained amplitude, and normalization that discards amplitude. Do not discard amplitude and then conclude that it is irrelevant. Output. An ambiguity gallery; height error by geometry/current subgroup; predictive spread on lookalikes; and a labelled subset of informative versus weakly informative cases. These cases should remain ﬁxed for comparing later models. 5.5 E04: the two-stage baseline Question. Is a simple height estimator followed by reconstruction suﬃcient? Train a CNN encoder with global pooling and an MLP receiving physical metadata. Predict h within the allowed training interval. Feed its estimate to a conditioned reconstructor trained with known heights. Evaluate a second variant in which the reconstructor is trained using noisy height estimates matching the predictor’s validation errors; otherwise a brittle two-stage baseline can make joint inference look unfairly strong. Compare height MAE, ﬁeld error, failure rate, and latency with the known-height counterparts. Repeat with at least several model seeds once the pilot is stable. Use the same prior capacity and training budget wherever feasible. 5.6 E05: joint ﬁeld–height reﬁnement Question. Does feedback between calibration and reconstruction add value? Start from the two-stage initialization, then perform a small trained number of physics-and-prior reﬁnement stages. Supervise both height and reference ﬁeld on simulation data; include observation consistency. Compare (a) frozen height, (b) gradient height updates, and (c) learned residual-based height updates. Control total parameter count and inference compute, not only stage count. Required ablations. Same reconstruction prior; identical metadata; same dataset; matched height initialization; no-reﬁnement model trained end to end; and a larger two-stage model under a similar compute budget. Log intermediate heights and errors to detect unstable oscillations or drift toward the bound. Decision gate Advance to a novel mechanism only if there is a reproducible residual failure: ambiguity, noise ampliﬁcation, scale mismatch, boundary inconsistency, or simulation-to-real mismatch. If the strong two-stage model solves the task, develop a diﬀerent scientiﬁc claim instead of obscuring it with added modules. 5.7 E06: multiple hypotheses and calibrated rejection Compare one height estimate with a coarse candidate bank and a shared conditional reconstructor. Preserve associated pairs (x j , h j ) instead of mixing unrelated image and height averages. Evaluate true-height set coverage, interval/set width, conditional coverage by geometry/noise, and the error on cases retained at increasing conﬁdence thresholds. Compare with a small ensemble and simple grid-search proﬁling. For discrete candidates, report the approximation error due to binning and include heights between 11 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction training bins. Use a separate calibration set for temperature scaling or conformal adjustments. The ability to return broad sets is useful only when informative cases remain narrow and diﬃcult cases are reliably ﬂagged. 5.8 E07: FOV, pitch, and outside-window contributions Use a full physical scene as the common parent. Create (i) diﬀerent crops at ﬁxed pitch, (ii) diﬀerent pitches at ﬁxed physical FOV, and (iii) diﬀerent FOVs at ﬁxed array dimensions. These are three diﬀerent shifts. Integrate and antialias before subsampling. Compare on registered common physical regions with documented target-grid conversion. Test sources touching the edge and sources just outside the window. Compare zero exterior, in- creased latent-domain support, and an explicit nuisance exterior model. Measure interior error, edge-band error, overlap disagreement, height bias, and predictive uncertainty. Cropping a propa- gated image is not equivalent to propagating a crop. 5.9 E08: noise and acquisition robustness Start with known white Gaussian noise as a controlled experiment, then add correlated noise, spatially varying variance, oﬀsets, and drift estimated from real repetitions. Keep physical noise level distinct from SNR; increasing height reduces signal even if instrument noise remains ﬁxed. Test both ﬁxed-noise and ﬁxed-SNR protocols, labelled separately. For repeated measurements, independent noise can support noise-to-noise denoising or adaptation, but does not by itself reveal frequencies removed by standoﬀ. Check shared calibration noise, ﬁtting-induced spatial correlation, and drift before assuming conditional independence. QDsiM [20] provides a noise-aware measurement simulation reference; adopting a simulator alone is not a methodological novelty. 5.10 E09: COMSOL-to-experiment transfer Match scalar NV projection versus vector input, units, sensor averaging, and acquisition back- grounds. Train on COMSOL, evaluate without adaptation, then compare calibration-only adap- tation and learned-prior adaptation on disjoint real sessions. Include a small real-only control if independently labelled height pairs are available. Separate gains from registration/calibration improvements from gains due to the new architecture. 5.11 E10: physical resolution and prior dependence Deﬁne a controlled feature family: for example two nearby track contributions, a narrow gap, or a small perturbation on a known source. Sweep separation and SNR at several heights. Deﬁne a detection or proﬁle criterion before locking the test set; report false positives and conﬁdence, not just visual sharpness. Compare ordinary interpolation to rule out claims based solely on increased output pixels. Perturb the learned prior with plausible out-of-distribution layouts. If features appear in the reconstruction without support in the measurement, test whether the uncertainty mechanism ﬂags them. A successful resolution claim must state the source family and measurement conditions under which it holds. 12 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction 5.12 E11: optional sensor tilt and eﬀective averaging If constant-height inference fails systematically across the FOV, use a low-dimensional tilted plane h(x, y) = h 0 + ax + by. Evaluate the physical ﬁeld on the nonplanar measurement coordinates and rotate the projection axis consistently when required. A spatial height map is not implemented by naively applying a diﬀerent local convolution at each pixel. Compare with a scalar eﬀective-height model on controlled simulated tilt and independently characterized acquisitions. 5.13 E12: optional multilayer source separation P Only after single-layer validation, model y = ℓ M h ℓ x ℓ + η, preferably with structural source priors or known template families. Use the Bathla dictionary as the known-source baseline. Add continuous depth/position corrections and test dictionary mismatch. Report cross-talk, activity errors, layer-parameter uncertainty, and information supplied at inference. Arbitrary layer images at arbitrary depths are not uniquely identiﬁable from one sum. E00–E01 Trusted physics + known-height baseline E02–E04 Wrong-height and am- biguity diagnostics E05 Joint prototype with strong controls E06 or E07 One failure- driven mechanism E08–E10 Noise, real data, re- liable resolution Figure 7: A research ladder with decision gates. E11–E12 are optional extensions, not prerequisites for completing the ﬁrst paper. Deliverable Maintain one experiment ledger with IDs E00–E12, question, control, split, conﬁguration hash, primary metrics, ﬁgure, conclusion, and next decision. A failed hypothesis is retained with its evidence. 6 What architectures to learn, build, and compare 6.1 A learning order tied to implementation milestones 13 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction Learn in order Concept and reference Implement and explain before moving on 1. Proximal inference ISTA/FISTA and LISTA [1]; ALISTA [2] 2. Residual CNN Signed regression and residual prediction 3. U-Net Multiscale encoder/decoder with skip paths [3] 4. Conditioning Feature modulation, e.g. FiLM [4] 5. Learned data consistency 6. Blind inference MoDL [5] and VarNet [6] as transferable patterns 7. Uncertainty Calibration [12]; conformal prediction [13] 8. Optional priors DIP [8], plug-and-play [9], FNO [10] Derive the gradient, adjoint, shrinkage, and step bound; distinguish optimization error from ﬁeld error. A small known-height ﬁeld reconstructor; linear output, correct units, sensible initialization. Compare local CNN and multiscale context; separate architecture choice from supervised training target. Condition on physical height/pitch/noise, and prove with an ablation that metadata improves transfer. Combine a learned prior with the exact measurement operator, including crop and projection. A bounded height update; diagnose prior-dependent calibration and degenerate solutions. Coverage and sharpness on a held-out calibration set; detect distribution-shift failures. Try only when the current failure suggests scan-speciﬁc ﬁtting, stronger priors, or operator transfer. Joint image/operator estimation [11] For each reading, write half a page: variables estimated, prior, measurement operator, information supplied at test time, data split, and a failure relevant to QDM. Architecture labels do not replace this analysis. 6.2 A0: reproduce the existing physics-correction LISTA The repository currently uses x k+1 = soft θ [x k − αA ∗ (Ax k − y) + C b y + C x x k ] . (9) Its two bias-free 9 × 9 single-channel corrections and scalar threshold are tied across layers. It has 163 trainable parameters, and zero corrections reproduce ISTA at initialization. H is ﬁxed in the current checkpoint/operator. Supervision targets sharp ﬁelds rather than sparse-optimization solutions; the distinction from original LISTA [1] matters. Useful ﬁrst ablations. Train versus zero correction; tied versus untied thresholds; input correc- tion versus state correction; scalar versus per-component threshold; same physical prior at several trained depths; blurred versus zero initialization. Compare accuracy–latency curves. A trained layer has extra convolutions, so it is not equal in cost to an ISTA iteration. Preserve the trained- depth restriction and do not infer convergence of learned updates. A controlled LISTA study you can run before the joint model. Use trained depths K ∈ {4, 8, 16} as an illustrative pilot grid, and compare (i) ﬁxed true-height ISTA/FISTA, (ii) 14 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction zero-correction LISTA, (iii) trained tied corrections, (iv) learn only steps/thresholds, and (v) un- tied corrections. Log ﬁeld error after each trained stage, physical residual, learned parameter changes, inference memory, and latency. Select the depth on validation sources. The ﬁxed-depth classical controls diagnose acceleration; epsilon-stopped classical controls diagnose optimization. They answer diﬀerent questions and should both be reported. A learned-FISTA control can introduce bounded trained momentum into the same physics update. Treat it as a ﬁxed-depth network; classical FISTA guarantees do not automatically apply to learned momentum or learned priors. If a compact step/threshold model matches a larger correction network, that is evidence to simplify the prior, not a reason to hide the smaller control. 6.3 A0b: coeﬃcient LISTA for the Bathla dictionary This is a distinct task with a genuinely sparse representation:   c k+1 = soft τ k c k + α k D T W T W (y − Dc k ) . (10) Learn bounded steps/thresholds ﬁrst, then consider learned corrections. Inputs are measured projected maps; outputs are coil coeﬃcients. Compare with LASSO, ridge, and applicable sign- constrained ﬁts using activation labels. Derive near-plane ﬁelds only through independently val- idated physical source templates. A measured sensor-plane basis cannot itself supply a sharp reference-plane basis. 6.4 A1: supervised residual CNN and U-Net controls Use a small residual CNN with approximately 4–6 convolutional blocks and 32–64 feature channels as an initial engineering conﬁguration. A U-Net control can use 3–4 scales and comparable capacity. Predict x̂ = x 0 +R θ (y, m) with a linear ﬁnal layer, where m is metadata and x 0 is a declared physical or observation-derived initialization. Train from scratch on magnetic data. Natural-image priors and pretrained RGB weights can impose unsuitable textures. Do not use sigmoid output for signed microtesla ﬁelds. Avoid hidden resizing, instance normalization that discards meaningful amplitude, and random-crop training that silently changes the forward boundary conditions. Compare ﬁxed amplitude metadata versus observation normalization with scale retained. Learn that a convolutional architecture is not automatically FOV/pitch invariant: a 9 × 9 kernel spans diﬀerent physical distances as pitch changes. Global pooling for height estimation can also hide how much of a source is visible. Test these issues rather than claiming invariance from variable tensor dimensions. 6.5 A2: known-height conditioned physics network Let r k = M h x k − y, and deﬁne u k = x k − α k M ∗ h W T W r k , x k+1 = u k + R θ (u k , M ∗ h W T W r k ; m). (11) (12) Condition the learned correction using a small metadata MLP. One FiLM-style implementation modulates feature channel j by γ j (m)z j + β j (m). Proposed metadata include physical ∆x, ∆y, gap, noise estimates, amplitude scale, projection/channel availability, and observation mask. Stan- dardize metadata using training statistics. Start with 6–8 stages, tied correction weights, and a conservative bounded step. These are pi- lot choices, not optimal hyperparameters. In a whitened problem the norm bound includes W , 15 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction sampling, and projection; do not reuse the bound for an unweighted convolution. Removing con- ditioning, physics gradients, or stage tying gives informative controls. An alternative MoDL-style data-consistency block solves (M ∗ h W T W M h + ρI)x k+1 = M ∗ h W T W y + ρD θ (x k ; m) (13) approximately using conjugate gradients. For padded/cropped operators, apply the true composi- tion rather than replacing it by multiplication with |H| 2 . Report CG accuracy and its contribution to runtime; keep ρ > 0. 6.6 A3: a strong two-stage calibration baseline A height encoder produces h 0 = h min + (h max − h min ) sigmoid(s ϕ (y, m)). Deﬁne this admissible physical interval independently of the training range; it can be broader than the training heights. Extrapolation tests must remain within the declared interval, and observations outside it are ﬂagged as unsupported. Feed the estimate to A2. Train the predictor on true simulation labels and the reconstructor ﬁrst on correct heights, then on realistic predictor errors. Jointly training the two blocks without iterative height feedback is a stronger control than freezing a poorly trained predictor. For a scalar NV input, use the proper projection in M h and a channel-availability mask. Vector outputs inferred from a scalar image require corresponding physical assumptions and can only be validated in channels with trusted reference data. Do not use current amplitude, source CAD, or true height in the network unless the inference regime declares them available. 6.7 A4: joint reﬁnement prototype Given (x k , h k ), perform the A2 ﬁeld update and reﬁne height. A physics-only candidate is g h,k = ⟨W r k , W ∂ h M h k x k ⟩ , (14) h k+1 = Π [h min ,h max ] (h k − β k g h,k ). (15) An alternative learns a bounded correction from r k , x k , metadata, and residual spectral summaries. Use explicit supervision for h and x during simulation training. The residual gradient is a useful feature, but does not resolve non-identiﬁability by itself. A learned source prior or source-latent representation supplies additional restrictions. Do not change the analytical operator with unconstrained learned ﬁlters and simultaneously call the resulting scalar a physical distance. If adding H eﬀ = H h + ∆H ψ , bound and calibrate ∆H ψ , check Hermitian symmetry/reality, and test whether the correction absorbs height. Compare the pure analytical model, a calibration-only correction, and a trained correction on source/session holdouts. 6.8 A5: a candidate bank for ambiguous height Choose an initial set of plausible heights {h j } Jj=1 and share the A2 reconstructor across candidates. Predict or optimize a ﬁeld x j for each, then score the pairs using measurement likelihood and a learned source prior. A conceptual Bayesian score is log p(h j , x j | y) ∝ − 12 W (M h j x j − y) 2 + log p θ (x j ) + log p(h j ). (16) This equation is not a justiﬁcation for calling arbitrary network logits a posterior. If p θ is unavail- able as a normalized density, label scores as predictive weights and calibrate empirically. Height classiﬁcation on true labels is a simple initial implementation. Then test continuous reﬁnement, bin-width eﬀects, and branch collapse. 16 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction y, pitch, projection, noise encoder initializes (x 0 , h 0 ) True forward/adjoint compute r k and ﬁeld gradient Conditioned learned prior update x k+1 Bounded height reﬁnement update h k+1 Repeat a trained number of stages return ﬁeld and cal- ibration estimate Figure 8: Proposed joint prototype. The exact operator handles known physics; the learned block encodes a data-dependent prior. Both height and reconstruction are trained and evaluated explicitly. Observed map + metadata h 1 shared inverse → x 1 h 2 shared inverse → x 2 h J shared inverse → x J Pair scoring + held- out calibration Height set and associated ﬁelds one mode only when supported Figure 9: A proposed uncertainty-aware inference route. Compare its extra compute with ensembles, proﬁling, and a stronger single-branch model. Candidate pairs should not be collapsed into unrelated mean image and mean height values. 17 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction 6.9 A6: uncertainty-sensitive spectral reﬁnement This is a hypothesis motivated by E02–E03, not a veriﬁed new method. For a gap uncertainty σ h , deﬁne sensitivity s(f ) = 2π ∥f ∥ σ h . A provisional gate might be w(f ) = 1/(1 + s(f ) 2 ), multiplied into the Fourier transform of a physics-gradient correction. Alternatively learn a gate conditioned on estimated spectral SNR, height distribution, and pixel spacing. Test ﬁxed low-pass gates, gates from true height error as an oracle diagnostic, and gates from predicted uncertainty. Gates can stabilize updates but also remove real detail. Derive their eﬀect on signed spectra, test feature false negatives, and compare under matched compute. Cropping means this frequency operation is an approximate reﬁnement/preconditioner, not an exact diagonalization of the whole observation operator. The candidate contribution is justiﬁed only if predicted uncertainty improves reliable detail recov- ery beyond simpler ﬁltering and existing conditioned priors. Do not claim that a hand-selected gate is physically optimal. 6.10 A7: current-latent inference as a stronger physical prior Predict a current stream function or parametrized conductor source, compute J, then use Biot– Savart to predict the measurement and the reference-plane ﬁeld. Train the primary loss on the near-plane ﬁeld. Where COMSOL supplies trusted J, add auxiliary current supervision as an explicitly available training signal. Compare with a ﬁeld-ﬁrst network receiving the same data. This representation reduces implausible independent-component outputs, but its assumptions may fail for contacts, ﬁnite thickness, vertical vias, or unknown multilayer sources. Geometry masks can be known metadata in one regime and unknown in another; report separate results. Recovering a latent J that ﬁts the ﬁeld does not prove unique current recovery. 6.11 Optional architectures: when they are worth trying Method Use when Main risk/control NAFNet-style restoration [7] Plug-and-play prior [9] Deep Image Prior [8] Fourier neural operator [10] Transformer or hybrid Diﬀusion/score prior [11] Need a strong eﬃcient CNN baseline Retrain for signed ﬁelds; compare physics integration and compute Denoiser need not minimize a known energy; test stability Scan-speciﬁc optimization can ﬁt noise; stopping cannot use test truth Mode truncation, domain extent, boundaries, and aliasing still matter More capacity is not novelty; matched strong CNN control Training/compute cost and plausible hallucinations; posterior calibration A magnetic-ﬁeld denoiser is reliable Paired sharp real data are scarce Resolution transfer remains a dominant failure Long-range source context matters beyond U-Net Multimodal source inference needs richer priors 6.12 How to turn a failure into an architectural hypothesis Use this chain: observation → mechanism → minimal change → controlled experiment → falsiﬁ- able claim. Example: the predictor confuses source width with distance; therefore test separate height hypotheses coupled to one physical inverse, and measure whether ambiguous cases receive 18 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction calibrated broad sets while ordinary cases retain accuracy. Compare against simply adding capac- ity. For the ﬁrst paper, the recommended route is A0/A1/A2 controls → A3 → A4 → one of A5 or A6 if the failures warrant it. A7 is a useful parallel scientiﬁc control when COMSOL current data are available; it should not double the entire project scope. Prior-informed joint calibration, FiLM, unrolling, ensembles, and diﬀusion are established ideas. Novelty must lie in an identiﬁable mechanism, analysis, and empirical evidence relative to relevant prior work, not the module names. Deliverable Keep a model card for every architecture: available inputs, estimated variables, prior, ex- act operator, trainable parameters, stage count, training objective, supervision, calibration method, latency, and excluded claims. 7 Training objectives and reliable evaluation 7.1 Supervision should match the intended claim For each simulation scene, store the reference ﬁeld x ⋆ , observation y, true h ⋆ , metadata m, and source identity. Where relevant store J ⋆ , but distinguish it from the main ﬁeld target. A proposed supervised objective is (17) L = L x + aL h + bL obs + cL aux , L x = L obs = ∥x̂ − x ⋆ ∥ 2 ∥x ⋆ ∥ 2 + ϵ  ,  L h = Huber ( ĥ − h ⋆ )/s h , (18) x 1 2 W (M ĥ x̂ − y) . n (19) Use a ﬁxed training-derived ﬂoor ϵ x for weak scenes and report such scenes separately. The scale s h makes height supervision interpretable. An auxiliary current loss is used only when a trusted current target exists. Loss weights are selected with the validation protocol, not the locked test set. For noisy targets, a noise-weighted likelihood is preferable to ﬁtting every sample exactly. Estimate W from calibration/repetitions, or use a speciﬁed synthetic covariance. Pixel independence and Gaussianity are assumptions, not consequences of a histogram. Finite-window model discrepancy can require a separate nuisance or robust residual model; inﬂating noise variance to hide every mismatch invalidates a physical accuracy claim. 7.2 Curriculum and optimization 1. Verify the forward/adjoint and height derivatives on tiny arrays. 2. Train A2 with known height on a stratiﬁed pilot. Inspect gradients, sign/amplitude conservation, and per-component errors. 3. Train the height predictor independently. Log error by source size/current and compare simple spectral features. 4. Train A3 end to end, including realistic height perturbations. This becomes the principal simple baseline. 5. Initialize A4 from A3; enable bounded height reﬁnement. Start with modest stage count and monitor each stage. 19 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction 6. Add one failure-driven mechanism. Reﬁt or freeze shared components according to an explicit ablation plan. 7. Expand COMSOL coverage, then add real calibration/adaptation on disjoint sessions. Adam or AdamW is a reasonable pilot optimizer; an illustrative initial learning-rate grid is 10 −4 to 10 −3 , with separate rates for small calibration heads if needed. Do not transfer the magnetization paper’s optimization schedule without justiﬁcation. Select architecture depth and epoch budget from validation learning curves. Prefer a short pilot over a large unsuccessful sweep. For learned updates, ﬁx the trained depth at inference unless extrapolation is itself evaluated. Classical solvers use the repository’s optimality-based stopping criterion with their actual update counts and stop reasons. Ground truth is used for reporting and supervised training, never for classical stopping or per-test regularizer selection. 7.3 Losses to add only with a reason Edge/proﬁle losses can prioritize narrow features but amplify target interpolation artifacts. Spec- tral losses require a deﬁned physical frequency grid and a reliability mask. SSIM is an optional supplementary metric; its data range and component treatment must be ﬁxed. A reconstruction that looks plausible while changing amplitudes may score well perceptually and still be scientif- ically wrong. Avoid an adversarial loss until ﬁeld amplitude, sign, and uncertainty are already controlled. For vector ﬁelds, a physically constrained latent potential/source may be stronger than an arbitrary penalty on components. A two-dimensional ﬁnite-diﬀerence divergence of (B x , B y ) is not the full three-dimensional condition ∇ · B = 0; the missing ∂ z B z matters. Enforce the appropriate source- free Fourier relations or full forward model rather than an incorrect 2D surrogate. 7.4 Uncertainty: what to predict and how to check it Distinguish measurement noise (aleatoric), source ambiguity, training uncertainty, and discrepancy in the measurement model. A small ensemble can probe model variability, but it is not a guarantee of Bayesian coverage. For a discrete height distribution, report cross-entropy or NLL, Brier score or reliability bins, height set coverage, and set width. For continuous estimates use calibrated intervals, coverage versus nominal conﬁdence, and sharpness. Conformal calibration [13] provides marginal coverage under its exchangeability assumptions. Hold- ing out an entirely diﬀerent source family or instrument can violate those assumptions. Report subgroup coverage under these shifts rather than implying a distribution-free guarantee still holds. Calibration and model selection must use separate data or a justiﬁed cross-validation scheme. Deﬁne a selective decision: accept a single-height reconstruction only when a calibrated height set and candidate ﬁelds are suﬃciently concentrated under a criterion ﬁxed on calibration data. Otherwise return the candidate set or label the result ambiguous. Evaluate the error–coverage curve as more diﬃcult cases are rejected. Rejection must not remove all useful scenes. P For a pair distribution with weights w j , the ﬁeld mean x̄ = j w j x j can minimize squared ﬁeld risk, P but (x̄, j w j h j ) need not be a physically coherent single explanation. Retain pairwise predictions for interpretation and repropagation. 7.5 Metrics and plots to standardize 20 QDM research playbook Quantity Physical RMSE Joint calibration and reconstruction Deﬁnition/use p Interpretation warning mean(x̂ − x ⋆ ) 2 in µT Relative L2 ∥x̂ − x ⋆ ∥ / ∥x ⋆ ∥ Range NRMSE RMSE divided by reference range Height MAE/bias mean | ĥ − h ⋆ | and signed bias in µm Proﬁles/features Peak amplitude, width, gap/separation, sign Whitened residual and spatial/spectral structure Registered disagreement on common physical support Coverage, set/interval width, selective error Warmed synchronized median and dispersion; memory Observation ﬁt FOV consistency Uncertainty Latency/resources Report components and predeﬁned ROI Unstable for negligible references; stratify Large backgrounds and extreme pixels aﬀect it Nominal/ﬁtted labels are not exact truth Predeﬁne proﬁle locations and criteria Small residual does not prove correct height Common crop agreement can hide common bias Validate under source and session shift Include height search/calibration stages Compute errors in physical units after reversing normalization. Report whole-FOV, interior, and source-region results with masks deﬁned from CAD or independent training rules, not selected to hide errors. For scalar real measurements, report measured-projection accuracy and reserve vector claims for independently validated channels. 7.6 A small evaluation matrix Test regime What changes Principal question In-distribution New source instances, familiar ranges Withheld topology/family or width/size range Interpolation and extrapolation separately Pitch or grid size, declared FOV Edge/exterior sources, partial views Covariance, variance, drift Basic estimator quality Geometry shift Height shift Sampling shift FOV shift Noise shift Real shift New coil/session/instrument where possible Does the prior generalize? Is calibration physically conditioned? Does scale information transfer? Are boundary assumptions appropriate? Is the estimator robust and calibrated? Does simulated training transfer? 7.7 Statistics, fairness, and reproducibility Use the physical scene/source or acquisition session as the unit of replication. Bootstrap paired method diﬀerences across sources, not millions of pixels as independent samples. Begin with at 21 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction least three model seeds for the ﬁnal selected variants if compute permits; report seed variability separately from source variability. Predeclare the primary endpoint and show conﬁdence intervals, failure cases, and practical eﬀect sizes. For timing, use identical hardware, dtype, batch size, output resolution, and observation informa- tion. Include candidate height search and uncertainty branches in total inference latency. Report training/calibration cost separately. A model with true height as input is an oracle diagnostic; label it clearly and do not mix it with unknown-height competitors. A method with test-time CAD or per-coil calibration has additional information and needs a separate evaluation regime. Save hashes for data manifests, splits, source code, checkpoints, and conﬁgurations. Record GPU model, software versions, numerical precision, stage counts, seeds, convergence outcomes, and any padding/support assumptions. Use fresh output directories; retain archived runs. A negative result is saved with its explanation rather than overwritten by a more favourable sweep. Deliverable A single evaluation script should produce component/ROI metrics, height distributions, un- certainty calibration, feature proﬁles, paired conﬁdence intervals, timing, and an HTML or PDF report from saved arrays. The test set is not a hyperparameter dashboard. 8 Experimental validation with the real microscope 8.1 Plan the ﬁrst campaign around one falsiﬁable claim The ﬁrst campaign should ask whether an unknown-height reconstruction improves a registered closer-plane prediction for sources excluded from ﬁtting/adaptation. Start with a few indepen- dently identiﬁable coil layouts, several sensor positions, repeated acquisitions, and at least two acquisition sessions if practical. Scale the number after a pilot establishes repeatability and uncer- tainty; a suggested count is an engineering starting point, not a statistical power calculation. For the archived multilayer array, use individual-coil activations to begin with a single active source and the corresponding background subtraction. Check whether routing, contacts, or wire bonds introduce sources between reference and sensor planes; simple source-free upward continuation is valid only above all relevant sources. A known layer depth can parameterize h ℓ = d 0 + z ℓ , but the common oﬀset d 0 still needs calibration or explicit inference. 8.2 A measurement protocol 1. Select a known layout and measure actual drive current, including sign and possible heating dependence. Record the source reference surface and relevant layer thicknesses. 2. Record a reference/background acquisition with the same optics, microwave settings, and sensor conﬁguration. 3. Acquire the closest usable plane, followed by several larger relative gaps. Record stage displace- ment, approach direction, mechanical repeatability, and drift. 4. At each position acquire repetitions or retain raw traces suﬃcient to estimate ﬁtting noise and covariance. Keep timestamps and acquisition order. 5. Repeat a subset at another session and on withheld layouts. Fit registration/calibration using designated calibration acquisitions, not every test target. 6. Construct registered observation–reference pairs only after checking coordinate transforms, mag- niﬁcation, projection axes, ﬁeld units, and averaging. 22 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction 8.3 What counts as height ground truth A calibrated stage increment establishes a relative displacement. It does not independently deter- mine NV implantation depth, physical contact gap, surface spacer thickness, or sample tilt. Report absolute height only where the complete reference is independently characterized, with error bars. Otherwise evaluate relative-gap estimation and near-plane prediction, and describe ﬁtted absolute distance as model-dependent. The magnetization study [18] is a useful conceptual reference for joint calibration with a physical prior, but its material model is not a coil prior. Its source-dependent calibration illustrates why nominal, model-ﬁtted, and independently measured distances belong in separate columns of the experimental report. 8.4 Near-plane reference versus optical-free ﬁeld If the closest measured image retains the optical PSF and NV-depth averaging, then it is a target for standoﬀ improvement under the same instrument, not automatically the true unblurred ﬁeld at 0.5 µm. Matching optics across height pairs helps isolate magnetic propagation, but changes in focus, magniﬁcation, and averaging must be logged. COMSOL near-plane truth is a separate evidence tier. For the ﬁrst paper, report both simulated ﬁeld-truth accuracy and experimental closer-plane mea- surement accuracy. Do not present the latter as complete optical deconvolution. If the physical z ref cannot be measured directly, state that restriction and validate the accessible target plane. 8.5 Domain adaptation without target leakage Use an adaptation split of real coils/sessions. Fit low-dimensional nuisance calibration ﬁrst: regis- tration, axis, gain, and relevant averaging. Then evaluate whether adapting the learned prior adds value beyond that calibration. Record all test-time optimization steps and include them in timing. Repeated noisy acquisitions can train a denoising consistency term if the source is unchanged and noise assumptions are supported. Unsupervised repropagation constrains the measurement but leaves the joint height–source ambiguity; combine it with validated priors or calibration information. A model trained against its own reconstruction cannot establish independent sharp-ﬁeld accuracy. 8.6 Multilayer extension and useful acquisition design When source drive is controllable, temporal coding can produce genuinely useful independent source information. Known, distinguishable excitation waveforms let you demodulate components before reconstructing each contribution. Design codes to improve conditioning under measured noise and acquisition budget, rather than merely collecting more redundant height planes. Test cross-talk and synchronization error. This can be a later co-design contribution, but dynamic source ﬁtting itself already exists in the group dataset. 9 A manageable 4–6 month work plan Period Main work Exit evidence Weeks 1–2 COMSOL audit; source splits; E00–E03; request archive metadata Trusted physics, wrong-height curves, ambiguity examples 23 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction Period Main work Exit evidence Weeks 3–4 E01/A0–A2; prior comparison; pilot learning curves A3 and A4; E04–E05; matched compute controls One candidate mechanism (A5 or A6); independent literature check E07–E09; real-data calibration/adaptation; acquisition pilot Locked evaluation; resolution and uncertainty; new height pairs Paper draft; targeted reviewer-style objections; additional controls Buﬀer for acquisition, revisions, release, and submission Strong known-height controls and quantitative failure diagnosis Demonstrated beneﬁt or rejection of joint reﬁnement A falsiﬁable contribution with matched ablation Transfer study and stable experimental protocol Weeks 5–6 Weeks 7–9 Weeks 10–12 Weeks 13–16 Weeks 17–20 Weeks 21–24 Independent evidence, failure cases, reproducibility Complete manuscript and documented limitations A venue-ready claim matched to actual results Dates are a planning range, not a promise. Conduct the real-data audit and acquisition scheduling early because external storage, calibration, and instrument time can be the critical path. Every week should yield a ﬁgure, table, operator check, or written decision rather than only more code. 9.1 Weekly operating rhythm 1. Write one question and a predicted outcome on Monday. 2. Run the smallest controlled experiment capable of disproving it. 3. Inspect source-level distributions, residuals, and diﬃcult examples. 4. On Friday write a one-page conclusion with the next decision. 5. Discuss that page with collaborators; update the experiment ledger. Limit active modelling changes to one at a time. When a result fails, decide whether the cause is measurement physics, optimization, source prior, or unavailable information before changing capacity. The strongest result may be a reliable failure detector or a well-supported resolution limit rather than a larger neural network. 10 From a prototype to a publishable contribution 24 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction Known drive/layout and source identity Calibration and background Height sweep and repetitions Field, distance, and reliability evidence Locked source/session test protocol Registration and noise audit Figure 10: New acquisitions complement the archive. Every arrow represents a recorded processing step, so measurement improvements and network improvements can be separated. 10.1 Write the evidence chain before the paper title Proposed claim Evidence required Main counterexample to test Joint inference helps A3 versus A4 with matched data/prior/compute Calibrated height sets; selective error Source/family/FOV/pitch holdouts Independent sessions/height pairs A larger or error-robust two-stage baseline wins High conﬁdence on lookalike unseen sources Hidden layout or amplitude shortcuts Gains explained solely by registration Plausible unsupported structure Handles ambiguity Generalizes physically Improves real QDM Recovers ﬁner detail Deﬁned feature task with false positives 10.2 Novelty audit For each proposed mechanism search both QDM/NV work and the broader inverse-imaging liter- ature. Joint source–height ﬁtting, unrolling, conditioning, Bayesian priors, and diﬀusion already have precedent. Write a comparison table of estimated variables, observation assumptions, prior, uncertainty, calibration, and evaluation regimes. The most important question is “what can our method do reliably that these methods cannot under comparable information?” Potential contributions are magnetic reﬁnement informed by uncertainty, joint source and height inference with calibrated rejection, or an explicit treatment of unknown sources outside the FOV. These are research hypotheses. Validate novelty before writing “ﬁrst” or “unexplored.” A physi- cally rigorous benchmark can be valuable, but a narrow same-sample training score is insuﬃcient evidence for the proposed generalization claim. 10.3 The minimum convincing paper package 1. One clearly deﬁned problem and primary output, with observational information speciﬁed. 2. One central new mechanism or analysis, motivated by a reproducible baseline failure. 3. A simulation benchmark split by source identity/family and a real validation protocol. 4. Strong classical, direct-learned, two-stage, and joint controls under comparable information. 5. Ablations, calibration sensitivity, geometry/noise challenge sets, source-level statistics, and hon- est failure cases. 25 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction 6. Available code/conﬁgurations/splits, or a documented substitute release if raw experimental data cannot be shared. Suggested paper ﬁgures: (1) ambiguity and task; (2) observation model and architecture; (3) wrong-height sensitivity; (4) baseline and joint comparisons; (5) unseen geometry/FOV/pitch; (6) uncertainty and selective risk; (7) experimental closer-plane predictions and proﬁles. Use only the ﬁgures supporting the actual central claim. Each caption should specify data provenance, split, physical units, and what information the method received. 10.4 Venue strategy and dated deadline snapshot The following are planning judgments, not acceptance requirements or guarantees. An experimental sensing talk and an archival algorithm paper also have dif- ferent publication requirements; check the actual call and prior-publication policy before planning both. 10.5 When to stop adding experiments Stop architectural expansion when the central claim has reproducible support, strong alternatives have been evaluated, and the main limitations are characterized. Complete documentation, visual 26 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction reporting, and the manuscript. Add a new experiment only if it resolves an objection material to the claim. A paper is improved by a coherent evidence chain, not the number of model acronyms. Deliverable At the end of month 3, write a two-page provisional paper argument: problem, prior work, proposed mechanism, strongest ﬁgure, hardest failure, and missing decisive evidence. Use it to choose the ﬁnal venue and remaining acquisitions. A Implementation map for the current repository A.1 What can be reused Existing ﬁle/area Reuse and required distinction Physical frequency convention and analytic transfer; extend observation modelling in a separate experiment. scripts/iterative.py Comparable ISTA/FISTA, objective/stationarity diagnostics, epsilon stopping, honest stop reasons. scripts/torch_inverse.py FFT mechanics and adjoint checks; current transfer is ﬁxed and single-channel, so a dynamic height operator needs a new implementation. scripts/lista.py Initialization-equivalent learned corrections, tied weights, checkpoint patterns, trained-depth semantics. scripts/compare_lista.py Training/timing/provenance patterns; replace same-sample kernel ﬁtting, truth-derived scaling, and training-only selection in the new benchmark. tests/ Existing numerical checks; extend only where new operator contracts, derivatives, projections, and sampling change. Crop and lambda reports Useful diagnostics and historical experiments; direct periodic crops are not a replacement for the new ﬁnite-window benchmark. Retain archived outputs. The proposed work is a new protocol and should not be compared as if old ﬁxed-iteration, empirical-kernel, same-sample runs used the same observation information. The existing COMSOL cache naming does not encode geometry identity; the expanded database requires a diﬀerent manifest/key scheme. scripts/propagator.py Suggested new modules: dataset_manifest.py, observation_model.py, joint_models.py, train_joint.py, evaluate_joint.py, and report_joint.py. These names describe a possible future organization; this document has not created or validated that training pipeline. A.2 A diﬀerentiable propagation fragment This example handles a symmetric padded ﬁeld operator only. Projection, pixel integration, un- equal latent/observation support, masks, and whitening must be composed separately with their correct adjoints. It demonstrates that the transfer is computed from a tensor height without converting it to NumPy or detaching it. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def propagate(x, h, dx_um, z_ref_um=0.5, pad=32): 27 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction # x: [batch, channels, H, W], signed fields # h: [batch], in um, kept in the autograd graph # dx_um: common physical pitch for this batch H0, W0 = x.shape[-2:] xp = F.pad(x, (pad, pad, pad, pad)) if pad else x ny, nx = xp.shape[-2:] fy = torch.fft.fftfreq(ny, d=dx_um, device=x.device, dtype=x.dtype) fx = torch.fft.fftfreq(nx, d=dx_um, device=x.device, dtype=x.dtype) freq = torch.sqrt(fy[:, None]**2 + fx[None, :]**2) gap = (h - z_ref_um).reshape(-1, 1, 1, 1) transfer = torch.exp(-2 * torch.pi * gap * freq) out = torch.fft.ifft2(torch.fft.fft2(xp) * transfer).real return out[..., pad:pad + H0, pad:pad + W0] # Validate positive gaps and pitch in the caller. # Cache frequency grids by shape/pitch/device/dtype, not H(h). # Different dx and dy require separate frequency spacings. For the same real radial transfer and symmetric support, the adjoint has the same pad/con- volve/crop form. That statement does not extend automatically to arbitrary C, S, or Q; their adjoints must insert residuals, transpose averaging, and transpose projection in reverse order. Check the implemented operator rather than assuming a transpose from its diagram. A.3 A split-aware training skeleton for batch in train_loader: y, truth, h_true, metadata = batch # metadata contains only information allowed at inference x_hat, h_hat = model(y, metadata) y_hat = observation_model(x_hat, h_hat, metadata) loss = field_loss(x_hat, truth) loss += weight_h * height_loss(h_hat, h_true) loss += weight_obs * observation_loss(y_hat, y, metadata) optimizer.zero_grad() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Select checkpoints using held-out validation sources. # Fit uncertainty calibration on a separate calibration split. # Evaluate the locked source/session test split after selection. The fragment is conceptual. It does not specify a novel architecture, justify the noise likelihood, or guarantee convergence. Simulation height labels are training supervision; never substitute true test height for a predicted estimate in the unknown-height result. B Practical records and templates B.1 Scene manifest example geometry_id: cad_hash_or_stable_layout_id scene_id: geometry_drive_mesh_id source_family: spiral_or_other_declared_family source_plane_definition: conductor_top_surface reference_height_um: 0.5 observation_height_um: 3.0 height_label_kind: exact_simulation_coordinate 28 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction height_uncertainty_um: 0.0 dx_um: 0.1 dy_um: 0.1 field_quantity: B field_unit: T components: [Bx, By, Bz] current_A: measured_or_prescribed_value grid_shape: [ny, nx] simulation_mesh_id: mesh_hash split_group: geometry_id_or_template_family parent_scene: full_physical_scene_id observation_transform: sensing_then_crop_version acquisition_session: null_for_simulation This example uses existing project units and a sample height pair. It is not a claim that every external database entry has those values. An experimental manifest should add NV axis, stage increments, absolute-height calibration method, raw-data references, lock-in/ODMR settings, drive logs, and measurement covariance identiﬁers. B.2 Experiment card ID and question: E___ / What would this experiment establish? Hypothesis and falsiﬁer: What outcome would reject the explanation? Inputs at inference: Height? CAD? dictionary? projection? pitch? Data and split: Source groups, acquisition sessions, manifest hashes. Method/control: One change; matched prior/data/compute. Primary endpoint: Field, height, resolution, or reliability criterion. Secondary diagnostics: Residual maps, proﬁles, spectra, timing. Result and uncertainty: Source-level eﬀect size and conﬁdence interval. Decision: Keep, reject, investigate physics, or acquire missing data. B.3 First 10 working days 1. Days 1–2: inventory the existing COMSOL database; deﬁne source identities, height origin, units, and available targets. Request the experimental archive and logs. 2. Days 3–4: freeze a pilot split; validate analytical propagation, adjoints, and height derivatives against small cases and several COMSOL pairs. 3. Days 5–6: produce known-height classical reconstructions and the wrong-height sweep. Examine boundary and spectral errors. 4. Days 7–8: form source–height lookalike pairs; vary source size/current independently. Write the ambiguity diagnosis. 5. Days 9–10: train a small known-height learned baseline or height predictor, depending on the diagnosis; draft the one-page next-experiment argument. The timetable assumes the COMSOL ﬁles can be read and paired. If the audit reveals inconsistent coordinates or missing targets, those corrections become the ﬁrst milestone. Do not start a month- long training campaign before the input contract is trusted. 29 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction B.4 Failure triage Symptom First investigation Height runs to a bound Non-identiﬁability, amplitude scaling, prior bias, sign of height derivative Regularization, unstable frequencies, wrong model, invalid height information Periodic assumption, source outside FOV, padding/support mismatch Units, normalization, NV projection, current sign, ﬁnal activation Registration, covariance, optical/NV averaging, raw readout artifacts Calibration leakage, narrow training family, unjustiﬁed likelihood, branch collapse Poor scores, insuﬃcient information, candidate spacing, untrained prior Weak control tuning, noisy height updates, redundant mechanism, excessive complexity Residual improves; truth worsens Crop seams or edge rings Wrong amplitudes/signs Good simulations; poor real maps Uncertainty always tiny Uncertainty always broad Joint model loses to two-stage B.5 A ﬁnal claim audit Before submission, ask whether the novelty is an algorithm, an uncertainty method, an observation model, or an experimental capability. State what was given at inference and what was estimated. Describe which ﬁne features were validated independently, which depend on priors, and whether the height reference is absolute or relative. Make “unseen geometry” mean excluded physical identities, not new crops of the same coil. Make “super-resolution” mean a deﬁned physical detail-recovery result, not a larger tensor. C Focused reading and questions for collaborators C.1 Read with an implementation target 1. LISTA and ALISTA: derive the layer from a proximal iteration and reproduce initialization equivalence [1, 2]. 2. U-Net and FiLM: build a multiscale signed-ﬁeld baseline, then test a single metadata- conditioning change [3, 4]. 3. MoDL/VarNet: implement exact data consistency for this observation model instead of copy- ing the MRI encoding [5, 6]. 4. QDM current reconstruction: identify the actual observation components, priors, and stand- oﬀ/noise comparisons [15, 16, 14]. 5. Bathla dictionary work: reproduce the available-data task and distinguish coeﬃcient sparsity from ﬁeld-pixel sparsity [17]. 6. Joint calibration and Bayesian source inference: map which assumptions stabilize the inverse [18, 19, 11]. 30 QDM research playbook Joint calibration and reconstruction 7. Calibration: implement coverage and selective-risk evaluation before adding a more complex posterior network [12, 13]. C.2 Questions to resolve when the hard disk arrives • Which maps are raw measurements, ﬁtted ﬁelds, averaged references, or dictionary reconstruc- tions? • Are all original basis maps and activation/drive labels available, and are actual currents recorded? • Are there repeated acquisitions, current-oﬀ data, raw ﬁt residuals, and timestamps? • Were heights independently calibrated, or estimated by a model? Which coordinate is the origin? • Which coils and layer depths are known, and which CAD variants have corresponding COMSOL models? • Do the archive’s measurements include a usable closer-plane reference, or should we acquire one? • Which arrays/sessions can be withheld for adaptation, calibration, and ﬁnal testing? These questions are operational metadata requirements. They do not require changing the agreed primary target or delaying the simulation pilot. References [1] K. Gregor and Y. LeCun.
